newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end mostly lower on wet forecasts.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end mostly lower on wet forecasts.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended mostly lower on Monday after long-range weather outlooks suggested a shift to a wetter pattern in the U.S. Midwest, traders said.
"Soybeans opened with lots of enthusiasm after they didn't see a lot of rain in downstate Illinois," Dean Witter analyst Jerry Gidel said.

"But they didn't factor in that through Friday we should see below normal temperatures and that the weekend was going to have the best opportunities for rain that we've had in the last week to 10 days."
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said in his daily update that a high pressure ridge would move west, increasing chances for rain in the U.S. Midwest.

"This morning's (Monday) computer guidance indicates that by this weekend and next week (the week of August 11) there will be some changes in the pattern," Davis wrote. "Plain and simply, this pattern is much more favorable for widespread rains in the central U.S."
Soybeans ended 9-1/4 cents per bushel lower to 3-1/4 cents higher with November down 9-1/4 at $6.46-1/4 a bushel and August up 3-1/4 at $7.65-1/4.

Monday's National Weather Service six- to 10-day outlook, released after the close of trading, confirmed Davis' forecast. The outlook called for below-normal temperatures and above-normal precipitation for Illinois.
World weather also drew bearish reviews. Rains fell in northern China over the weekend, easing concerns of heat and moisture stress.
"Beans got whacked because of the good rains that occured across the northern provinces of China," Dean Witter's Gidel said. "We've stablized those conditions for a while."

August drew strength from the lack of deliveries posted against the August on Monday. Soybean registrations stood at 65,000 bushels total in the three deliverable locations, CBOT said Monday afternoon.
Friday's Commodity Futures Trading Commission Commitments of Traders report held few surprises, the traders said.
It confirmed that since Tuesday, funds were getting long corn and shorts were starting to get run out of beans, a trader said.

The CFTC said as of Tuesday, non-commercials, including funds were long soybeans 63.570 million bushels and short by 122.1 million. Commercials were long by 329.280 million bushels and short by 271.505 million.

On the day, funds sold at least 25 million bushels of soybeans. Prudential Securities and Refco Inc each sold at least seven million bushels November, Rosenthal Collins and O'Connor and Co each sold four million NOvember and Term Commodities sold three million November.
In options, FIMAT Futures sold 700 November $7.00 calls at 20 to 20-1/2 cents. Prudential Securities bought 500 November $6.00 puts at 11 cents and sold 500 November $5.50 puts at three cents.
Volatility in the November was pegged at 28 percent, down from 34 percent on Friday.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 56,000 contracts, compared with Friday's actual volume of 47,488. Options volume was pegged at 25,000 contracts, against Friday's 34,072.
